analysis.one_liner: Charges the largest fossil fuel companies $1 trillion to fund climate disaster recovery and resilience.
analysis.headline: The bill would collect a one-time $1 trillion assessment from the largest fossil fuel companies, but it has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since January 2025 with 6 cosponsors and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge companies that extracted or refined fossil fuels responsible for more than a billion metric tons of carbon dioxide between 2000 and 2023 a share of a one-time $1 trillion assessment, due by September 2026 or in nine annual installments. The money would go into a new trust fund paying for climate disaster recovery, resilient infrastructure, and help for communities hit hardest by climate change and pollution, including a 40% set-aside for environmental justice communities. The bill also explicitly preserves lawsuits against fossil fuel companies under state law.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by climate disasters, including through at least $15 billion a year to FEMA for disaster response and resilience and $6 billion a year in Clean Air Act grants, plus funding for resilient energy, water, farming, and transportation systems. Forty percent of annual spending is set aside for environmental justice communities — communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities that bear the worst effects of pollution and extreme weather. Federal and state taxpayers also benefit because climate costs now covered by general revenue would be paid by fossil fuel companies, and the bill preserves state-law lawsuits against the industry.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities facing climate disasters and pollution

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new Polluters Pay Climate Fund in the Treasury, filled by the $1 trillion assessment, and spends it on climate resilience, adaptation, disaster response, and environmental justice — including disaster recovery and mitigation, climate-resilient infrastructure, grid resilience, climate-resilient farming, wildfire management, extreme heat public health programs, and drinking water systems.

Guarantees at least $15 billion a year to FEMA for climate disaster response and resilience (including at least $3 billion for the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program) and at least $6 billion a year in Clean Air Act grants, with 40% of annual fund spending reserved for environmental justice communities.

Targets only the largest polluters: companies are assessed in proportion to their share of covered emissions and only if they were responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2000 through 2023, with joint and several liability across corporate controlled groups so companies cannot dodge the bill by splitting up.

Explicitly does not preempt state and local climate laws and preserves private, state, local, and Tribal lawsuits against fossil fuel companies for deception, nuisance, negligence, and other climate-related claims — and fund payments cannot be used to offset any court damages.

analysis.who_pays: The handful of the largest fossil fuel extraction and refining companies operating in the United States — US and foreign-owned — that the Treasury Secretary determines are responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emitted from their operations and products between January 1, 2000 and December 31, 2023. They owe a share of $1 trillion by September 30, 2026, or in nine annual installments starting with 20% of the total, and the assessment cannot be deducted from other federal taxes. Some of the cost would likely be passed to consumers through fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Largest oil, gas, and coal companies

drawbacks.text: Fossil fuel companies would likely pass much of the assessment to consumers through higher prices for gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity, so ordinary households would bear part of the cost even though the tax is levied on the companies.

The assessment is retroactive: it covers emissions released between 2000 and 2023 under rules in force at the time, a one-time charge on past activity that industry would challenge in court even though the bill states it is not a determination of fault and preserves other legal claims.

Money only moves if Congress appropriates it: the fund's spending is 'available, as provided in appropriations Acts,' so a future Congress could leave the money in the Treasury and communities would see none of the promised resilience and recovery funding.

The bill concentrates the charge on companies above the 1-billion-ton threshold, using Treasury formulas for attributing past emissions, which invites years of litigation over the exact share each company owes and over successor liability for companies that have merged or restructured.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would shift roughly $1 trillion of climate costs now carried by taxpayers onto the companies that extracted and refined the fuels, while funding disaster recovery and resilience for communities that need it — a large benefit concentrated on climate-vulnerable places and a cost on a small set of very profitable companies. The real drawbacks are that part of the cost would reach consumers through fuel prices, the retroactive design invites legal challenge, and every dollar is hostage to future appropriations votes. It is a well-targeted but hard-to-enforce bill, and its biggest weakness so far is political: almost no support beyond its six original sponsors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in January 2025 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has not held a hearing, marked it up, or voted on it.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Van Hollen introduced the bill on January 7, 2025, joined by Senators Sanders, Merkley, Markey, and Warren, on the first day of the new Congress.

The bill would impose a one-time $1 trillion assessment, divided among companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2000 through 2023, with payment due September 30, 2026 or in nine annual installments.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the public record shows no further action since.
Cosponsorship has grown to six senators — five Democrats and one of the Senate's two independents — with no Republican support and no committee action 20 months into the two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest fossil fuel companies, which so far owe nothing under the bill, and the senators and committee leadership who face no political cost from leaving it unaddressed; the cost of climate disasters continues to fall on general federal taxpayers and on the communities hit by floods, fires, and heat.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Largest fossil fuel companies, so far

for.role: Original cosponsors (Merkley, Markey, Warren, and others)

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Holds 55 of 100 Senate seats and all committee chairships
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator has cosponsored the bill, and the majority sets the Senate's agenda, including which bills get committee time and floor votes.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry trade groups
against.role: Oil, gas, and coal industry lobbying organizations
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed legislation that charges fossil fuel companies for climate damages, including retroactive 'polluter pays' assessments like this one.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors are Democrats or the Senate's independents, no Republican has signed on, and the Republican majority controls the Finance Committee where the bill sits; no vote has occurred yet, so the partisan split is inferred from sponsorship and committee control.

industries.industry: Oil and gas extraction and refining
industries.note: The bill's core charge falls on the largest companies in this industry: a share of a $1 trillion assessment based on their emissions from 2000-2023, with joint and several liability across corporate groups and no tax deduction. Its interest runs against the bill's public purpose, since the assessment shifts climate costs from taxpayers onto the industry.
Coal extraction is explicitly covered; major coal producers above the 1-billion-ton emissions threshold would owe their proportional share of the $1 trillion assessment.

Consumers would fund the public benefit partly through higher fuel prices if companies pass the assessment through, but they also gain from funded disaster recovery and resilience programs. The bill's benefits are broader than its consumer cost, though low-income households feel fuel price increases hardest.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding a 55-seat Senate majority, chairing the Finance Committee, and not one Republican cosponsor, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or markup this Congress. Barring an unexpected political shift, it will die quietly in committee at the end of the 119th Congress, as large revenue-raising bills from the minority party typically do.
